body: Mediocre for the price. Pictures OK, Sounds OK. Does not support FreelyTV - but that is partly the fault of the way Freely is implemented. Live channel information and program guide is very flaky and unreliable. At least 50% of the time, the TV can not tell you what programme is currently playing or what/when the next program will be. This is frustrating, but the real kicker is that you can not change channel when the information is not available - the TV can not 'remember' what the channel map is, so if you try to go to a channel and there is no 'current' information, then the TV refuses to change channel. This is infuriating. You have to resort to scrolling through a hundred channels to reach the one you are interested in - and then if you don't want to watch it - you have to scroll all the way back again. I guess TVs are aiming themselves at streaming services and don't care about live broadcast channels any more. If you shut this TV off while watching a live channel, then turn it back on, it reverts to the digital streaming home page, rather than opening the channel you were previously watching. Overall - the TV is fine - but it has been a very underwhelming experience, and I wish I had saved some money.

body:
I’ve spent some time looking into the 55-inch LG C5 OLED evo AI 4K Smart TV, and honestly—it’s one of those TVs that’s just really easy to like.

The first thing you notice is the picture. It looks seriously good. Blacks are properly black (not that washed-out grey you get on cheaper TVs), and colours pop without looking fake. Watching movies on it feels a bit more “cinema-like,” especially in a dim room. It’s also brighter than older LG C-series models, which helps if you’re not always watching in the dark.

Where it really surprised me is gaming. If you’ve got a PS5 or Xbox, this thing is kind of a dream—super smooth, very responsive, and it supports all the modern features without any fuss. It just works, and it works well.

The smart TV side is solid too. LG’s interface isn’t perfect, but it’s fast enough and has all the apps you’d expect, so you’re not fighting the system just to watch something.
That said, it’s not flawless. The sound is… fine. Not bad, but definitely not impressive—you’ll probably end up wanting a soundbar. And while it’s bright for an OLED, it’s not the brightest TV out there, so if your room gets a lot of sunlight, that’s something to keep in mind.

It’s a really well-rounded TV. Nothing about it feels gimmicky—it just delivers great picture quality, excellent gaming performance, and a smooth everyday experience. If you want a premium TV without overthinking it too much, the C5 is a very safe bet.

body:
I recently bought the LG 65” C5 OLED, and after spending some time with it, I can honestly say it’s one of the best TVs I’ve ever owned.

The picture quality is phenomenal. The OLED panel delivers perfect blacks and incredible contrast, which makes movies and shows look stunning, especially in dark scenes. My favourite profile is Filmmaker Mode giving near accurate colours, and the level of detail in 4K content is outstanding. Watching Dolby Vision content on this TV genuinely feels cinematic.

The brightness is impressive for an OLED especially after the recent firmware update.

For gaming, this TV is fantastic. With HDMI 2.1 ports, 4K at 120Hz, VRR, and extremely low input lag, it pairs perfectly with my PS5. Motion is smooth and responsive, making fast-paced games feel incredibly fluid.

The webOS interface is fast and easy to use, with all the major streaming apps available. Navigation is smooth, and the Magic Remote makes browsing and searching surprisingly easy.

Overall, the LG C5 65” delivers exceptional picture quality, top-tier gaming performance, and a premium design. If you're looking for a high-end OLED TV that excels for movies, streaming, and gaming, this one is absolutely worth it.

body: I chose this model because it was highly rated by Which?, to replace a TV that was 9 years old. The picture quality is the really stand-out thing compared to the TV I'm replacing: it's exceptional, vivid, and the blacks are true black. The TV definitely warrants a 5 star for picture quality.The sound is fine, it's clear and I've no complaints about the depth or bass. We don't have a soundbar, and I don't feel a need to get one.The only reason I scored the TV 4 stars rather than 5, are the menus and to some extent, the magic remote. I'm definitely tech savvy, but it's taken me a few days to find my way around fundamental functions on the TV (e.g. I found it easier to set up "favourite channels", but then it took another couple of days to figure out how to actually access "favourites"). I like the pointer on the Magic Remote, which definitely makes things easier, but the remote is let down by a very simple design flaw: both the "volume up/down" and the "channel up/down" buttons are pure black rubber. There is no visual marking on the buttons, so it's hard to see which is which. I know I'll get used to is, but in the meantime I've actually put a dab of white paint on the +/- and up/down symbols so that they are visible. The menu itself is cluttered, and there doesn't seem to be a way of hiding some the channels (e.g. I've no need for the LG channel at present, and we don't subscribe to channels like Disney, so those apps don't need to be visible on my list ... but they are, and they make it look cluttered.Overall, this is a BRILLIANT TV, and if you can put up with a cluttered menu, an overly-complex system for watching TV, and a good but imperfect remote, then I would recommend this.

body:
This review is for the 42" C55LA - Genuinely beautiful screen and picture quality. I spent ages researching this TV before buying and went to see various TV's in person in a Curry's before purchasing directly from LG online. The OLED display on the C5 looked night and day better than pretty much all of the other screens in store. It looked marginally better than the main rival's OLED display but I noticed odd flickering on the other brand's OLED on certain scenes (across various TV's) and also felt that the build and material quality of the LG C5 was significantly more premium than that of its rival at this size.The 42" is perfect for our space, and it looks awesome - super thin and really nice thin bezel. 
All in all picture quality - deep blacks - super nice with films and even standard TV - looks brilliant.The only downsides are -UK version ships with a pretty poor remote - it feels cheap and it's poorly laid out + very clunky and big. I believe the rest of the world get a nicer remote..
The OS is a bit cumbersome and bloated - there's a few tweaks to make it less so but it's still not a very nice experience. Also the remote cursor thing is genuinely annoying - you should be able to turn that off.
The other downsides are the audio quality - obviously this is a thin device but the audio is poorer than I expected it to be, and I didn't have much home in the first place + the legs that the TV stands on (42" version) are a bit flimsy but they look good.None of the downsides overshadow what is genuinely an unbelievable device with outstanding picture quality (which I find plenty bright btw). If you can get a good deal on this TV just buy it - it's a genuinely wonderful device despite its minor shortcomings.

The new opperating system takes a bit of getting use to, but is a lot better as you can customise more.

body: It is a very wonderful product with a clear picture, good sound quality and we are enjoying the product.

I expected far more from this TV, especially considering the price.

The OLED panel does provide excellent contrast and a very sharp picture, but in my experience the colour reproduction is disappointing. I have tried numerous picture modes and settings, yet I still cannot get the image to look as natural as I would expect from a premium television.

The sound quality is also poor. In fact, I have older TVs that sound noticeably better, which is difficult to justify on a product at this price level.

My biggest issue, though, is how unnecessarily complicated LG has made the whole experience. There are far too many menus, settings, options and customisations for what should be a simple household device. I work in IT and am very comfortable with technology, yet I have still found this TV frustrating to set up and difficult to configure exactly how I want it.

There is also too much LG advertising and promotional content built into the interface, along with screensavers and other features that are far harder to disable than they should be.

The TV feels like a product designed by engineers who have forgotten that most people simply want to switch it on, watch something and have it look and sound good. Instead, LG has turned a basic everyday item into something unnecessarily complex and over engineered.

I would be particularly concerned about recommending this to an older person or anyone who is not confident with technology, as I think many people would find the setup and menu system overwhelming.

For the money, I expected excellent picture quality, good sound and a polished, simple user experience. What I got was impressive contrast, disappointing colour, poor sound and an interface that constantly gets in the way.

At this price, that is simply not good enough.

I would not recommend this TV.

body: Best TV I've ever had. Picture quality is excellent.

The smart TV features are intuitive and easy to use. LG's webOS platform is fast, responsive, and provides access to all the major streaming services. Navigation is straightforward, and the Magic Remote makes finding content effortless.

The design is sleek, modern, and premium-looking. Its ultra-thin profile and minimal bezels allow the screen to take centre stage and look fantastic in any living room.

Overall, the LG OLED65C55LA delivers exceptional performance across the board. The combination of stunning OLED picture quality, excellent gaming features, user-friendly smart functionality, and elegant design makes it one of the best televisions I've ever owned. Highly recommended to anyone looking for a premium TV experience that truly impresses every time you switch it on.

body: Mediocre for the price. Pictures OK, Sounds OK. Does not support FreelyTV - but that is partly the fault of the way Freely is implemented. Live channel information and program guide is very flaky and unreliable. At least 50% of the time, the TV can not tell you what programme is currently playing or what/when the next program will be. This is frustrating, but the real kicker is that you can not change channel when the information is not available - the TV can not 'remember' what the channel map is, so if you try to go to a channel and there is no 'current' information, then the TV refuses to change channel. This is infuriating. You have to resort to scrolling through a hundred channels to reach the one you are interested in - and then if you don't want to watch it - you have to scroll all the way back again. I guess TVs are aiming themselves at streaming services and don't care about live broadcast channels any more. If you shut this TV off while watching a live channel, then turn it back on, it reverts to the digital streaming home page, rather than opening the channel you were previously watching. Overall - the TV is fine - but it has been a very underwhelming experience, and I wish I had saved some money.

body:
I’ve spent some time looking into the 55-inch LG C5 OLED evo AI 4K Smart TV, and honestly—it’s one of those TVs that’s just really easy to like.

The first thing you notice is the picture. It looks seriously good. Blacks are properly black (not that washed-out grey you get on cheaper TVs), and colours pop without looking fake. Watching movies on it feels a bit more “cinema-like,” especially in a dim room. It’s also brighter than older LG C-series models, which helps if you’re not always watching in the dark.

Where it really surprised me is gaming. If you’ve got a PS5 or Xbox, this thing is kind of a dream—super smooth, very responsive, and it supports all the modern features without any fuss. It just works, and it works well.

The smart TV side is solid too. LG’s interface isn’t perfect, but it’s fast enough and has all the apps you’d expect, so you’re not fighting the system just to watch something.
That said, it’s not flawless. The sound is… fine. Not bad, but definitely not impressive—you’ll probably end up wanting a soundbar. And while it’s bright for an OLED, it’s not the brightest TV out there, so if your room gets a lot of sunlight, that’s something to keep in mind.

It’s a really well-rounded TV. Nothing about it feels gimmicky—it just delivers great picture quality, excellent gaming performance, and a smooth everyday experience. If you want a premium TV without overthinking it too much, the C5 is a very safe bet.

body:
I recently bought the LG 65” C5 OLED, and after spending some time with it, I can honestly say it’s one of the best TVs I’ve ever owned.

The picture quality is phenomenal. The OLED panel delivers perfect blacks and incredible contrast, which makes movies and shows look stunning, especially in dark scenes. My favourite profile is Filmmaker Mode giving near accurate colours, and the level of detail in 4K content is outstanding. Watching Dolby Vision content on this TV genuinely feels cinematic.

The brightness is impressive for an OLED especially after the recent firmware update.

For gaming, this TV is fantastic. With HDMI 2.1 ports, 4K at 120Hz, VRR, and extremely low input lag, it pairs perfectly with my PS5. Motion is smooth and responsive, making fast-paced games feel incredibly fluid.

The webOS interface is fast and easy to use, with all the major streaming apps available. Navigation is smooth, and the Magic Remote makes browsing and searching surprisingly easy.

Overall, the LG C5 65” delivers exceptional picture quality, top-tier gaming performance, and a premium design. If you're looking for a high-end OLED TV that excels for movies, streaming, and gaming, this one is absolutely worth it.

Gaming performance is also top-tier with low input lag and flawless support for next-gen consoles. webOS is fast, intuitive, and far more responsive than the smart system on my previous TV. Apps load quickly and the interface is clean and easy to navigate. The design itself is sleek and premium, with incredibly thin bezels that really let the picture take centre stage. I was a bit unsure about losing Ambilight, but the sheer quality of the display more than makes up for it. This TV feels like a proper step into the high-end OLED experience. Highly recommended.

body: I chose this model because it was highly rated by Which?, to replace a TV that was 9 years old. The picture quality is the really stand-out thing compared to the TV I'm replacing: it's exceptional, vivid, and the blacks are true black. The TV definitely warrants a 5 star for picture quality.The sound is fine, it's clear and I've no complaints about the depth or bass. We don't have a soundbar, and I don't feel a need to get one.The only reason I scored the TV 4 stars rather than 5, are the menus and to some extent, the magic remote. I'm definitely tech savvy, but it's taken me a few days to find my way around fundamental functions on the TV (e.g. I found it easier to set up "favourite channels", but then it took another couple of days to figure out how to actually access "favourites"). I like the pointer on the Magic Remote, which definitely makes things easier, but the remote is let down by a very simple design flaw: both the "volume up/down" and the "channel up/down" buttons are pure black rubber. There is no visual marking on the buttons, so it's hard to see which is which. I know I'll get used to is, but in the meantime I've actually put a dab of white paint on the +/- and up/down symbols so that they are visible. The menu itself is cluttered, and there doesn't seem to be a way of hiding some the channels (e.g. I've no need for the LG channel at present, and we don't subscribe to channels like Disney, so those apps don't need to be visible on my list ... but they are, and they make it look cluttered.Overall, this is a BRILLIANT TV, and if you can put up with a cluttered menu, an overly-complex system for watching TV, and a good but imperfect remote, then I would recommend this.

body:
This review is for the 42" C55LA - Genuinely beautiful screen and picture quality. I spent ages researching this TV before buying and went to see various TV's in person in a Curry's before purchasing directly from LG online. The OLED display on the C5 looked night and day better than pretty much all of the other screens in store. It looked marginally better than the main rival's OLED display but I noticed odd flickering on the other brand's OLED on certain scenes (across various TV's) and also felt that the build and material quality of the LG C5 was significantly more premium than that of its rival at this size.The 42" is perfect for our space, and it looks awesome - super thin and really nice thin bezel. 
All in all picture quality - deep blacks - super nice with films and even standard TV - looks brilliant.The only downsides are -UK version ships with a pretty poor remote - it feels cheap and it's poorly laid out + very clunky and big. I believe the rest of the world get a nicer remote..
The OS is a bit cumbersome and bloated - there's a few tweaks to make it less so but it's still not a very nice experience. Also the remote cursor thing is genuinely annoying - you should be able to turn that off.
The other downsides are the audio quality - obviously this is a thin device but the audio is poorer than I expected it to be, and I didn't have much home in the first place + the legs that the TV stands on (42" version) are a bit flimsy but they look good.None of the downsides overshadow what is genuinely an unbelievable device with outstanding picture quality (which I find plenty bright btw). If you can get a good deal on this TV just buy it - it's a genuinely wonderful device despite its minor shortcomings.

body:
Purchased the LG 77 C5 to replace my LG 65 CX. Nothing wrong with the CX just wanted to go bigger. As I already owned a OLED tv I wasnt expecting a big wow factor as I did when I went from a LED.
The C5 blew me away. The picture quality is awesome and colours are so strong and the blacks are blacks. With the older CX I had to close the blinds to reduce the glare, but what ever they have done to reduce the glare and make the screen brighter definitely works. 
Another issue with the CX was dark scenes it was sometimes hard to make out details but this is now not an issue on the C5. 
Sound is also a lot better on the C5 but I use a sound bar so this was something that wasnt going to change.
The new opperating system takes a bit of getting use to, but is a lot better as you can customise more.
The remote has lost a few buttons and is a little slimmer. In all honestly for such and expensive tv the remote looks and feels cheap, but you dont buy a tv for the remote.
Last point a few changes to make straight away. Use film maker mode for all media and also switch of energy saving mode. You want the full brightness as thats why you paid for.

body: Setup is a bit complicated, picture quality is excellent.

I upgraded to this 55-inch LG B5 OLED from an older 55-inch LG 4K television that had served us well for many years. The improvement is immediately noticeable. The picture is incredibly sharp, colours are rich, motion is smooth and the black levels make films and streaming programmes look particularly impressive. We use the television for a mixture of Sky Q, Netflix, Prime Video and general family viewing, and it performs very well across all of them. Sky Q works perfectly in 2160p UHD, while HD programmes are also presented clearly. The menus and smart features are responsive, and setup was straightforward. The screen was initially brighter and more intense than we were used to, particularly in our fairly dark living room, but the extensive picture controls made it easy to adjust the OLED brightness and colour temperature to suit our eyes. Once set up properly, the picture is both comfortable and excellent. It also fitted securely onto our existing motorised VESA wall mount and works well with our older LG soundbar through the optical connection. Most importantly, I purchased it directly from LG at an excellent promotional price. For the picture quality, features and 120Hz OLED panel, it represents amazing value. I am extremely pleased with the upgrade and hope it serves us as reliably as our previous LG television.

Thankfully after much digging I found the menu options to get them off my screen, but they should not be there in the first place.The new remote is awful, the old one had buttons to pause and play and skip forward and back readily there. New one does not, for no conceivable reason, especially with the amount of apps people use.Lastly - the included Copilot that I cannot uninstall. Get that trash off my machine, I don't want it, I don't need it, it only takes space I could use for other things. Give me an option to deduct the license fee and get it off the TV, honestly.So much stuff added and still no option to make the TV just boot up YouTube or any other app instead of starting off on the tv channels/menu. Surely that kind of software update isn't impossible, I know so many people have asked for this option for years on official forums.All in all, the hardware of the TV is great, but if I knew the amount of bad software I'd get on it and not able to remove, I would have probably kept my old TV.

body: It is a very wonderful product with a clear picture, good sound quality and we are enjoying the product.

I expected far more from this TV, especially considering the price.

The OLED panel does provide excellent contrast and a very sharp picture, but in my experience the colour reproduction is disappointing. I have tried numerous picture modes and settings, yet I still cannot get the image to look as natural as I would expect from a premium television.

The sound quality is also poor. In fact, I have older TVs that sound noticeably better, which is difficult to justify on a product at this price level.

My biggest issue, though, is how unnecessarily complicated LG has made the whole experience. There are far too many menus, settings, options and customisations for what should be a simple household device. I work in IT and am very comfortable with technology, yet I have still found this TV frustrating to set up and difficult to configure exactly how I want it.

There is also too much LG advertising and promotional content built into the interface, along with screensavers and other features that are far harder to disable than they should be.

The TV feels like a product designed by engineers who have forgotten that most people simply want to switch it on, watch something and have it look and sound good. Instead, LG has turned a basic everyday item into something unnecessarily complex and over engineered.

I would be particularly concerned about recommending this to an older person or anyone who is not confident with technology, as I think many people would find the setup and menu system overwhelming.

For the money, I expected excellent picture quality, good sound and a polished, simple user experience. What I got was impressive contrast, disappointing colour, poor sound and an interface that constantly gets in the way.

At this price, that is simply not good enough.

I would not recommend this TV.

The design is sleek, modern, and premium-looking. Its ultra-thin profile and minimal bezels allow the screen to take centre stage and look fantastic in any living room.

body:
I’ve spent some time looking into the 55-inch LG C5 OLED evo AI 4K Smart TV, and honestly—it’s one of those TVs that’s just really easy to like.

The first thing you notice is the picture. It looks seriously good. Blacks are properly black (not that washed-out grey you get on cheaper TVs), and colours pop without looking fake. Watching movies on it feels a bit more “cinema-like,” especially in a dim room. It’s also brighter than older LG C-series models, which helps if you’re not always watching in the dark.

Where it really surprised me is gaming. If you’ve got a PS5 or Xbox, this thing is kind of a dream—super smooth, very responsive, and it supports all the modern features without any fuss. It just works, and it works well.

The smart TV side is solid too. LG’s interface isn’t perfect, but it’s fast enough and has all the apps you’d expect, so you’re not fighting the system just to watch something.
That said, it’s not flawless. The sound is… fine. Not bad, but definitely not impressive—you’ll probably end up wanting a soundbar. And while it’s bright for an OLED, it’s not the brightest TV out there, so if your room gets a lot of sunlight, that’s something to keep in mind.

It’s a really well-rounded TV. Nothing about it feels gimmicky—it just delivers great picture quality, excellent gaming performance, and a smooth everyday experience. If you want a premium TV without overthinking it too much, the C5 is a very safe bet.

body:
I recently bought the LG 65” C5 OLED, and after spending some time with it, I can honestly say it’s one of the best TVs I’ve ever owned.

The picture quality is phenomenal. The OLED panel delivers perfect blacks and incredible contrast, which makes movies and shows look stunning, especially in dark scenes. My favourite profile is Filmmaker Mode giving near accurate colours, and the level of detail in 4K content is outstanding. Watching Dolby Vision content on this TV genuinely feels cinematic.

The brightness is impressive for an OLED especially after the recent firmware update.

For gaming, this TV is fantastic. With HDMI 2.1 ports, 4K at 120Hz, VRR, and extremely low input lag, it pairs perfectly with my PS5. Motion is smooth and responsive, making fast-paced games feel incredibly fluid.

The webOS interface is fast and easy to use, with all the major streaming apps available. Navigation is smooth, and the Magic Remote makes browsing and searching surprisingly easy.

Overall, the LG C5 65” delivers exceptional picture quality, top-tier gaming performance, and a premium design. If you're looking for a high-end OLED TV that excels for movies, streaming, and gaming, this one is absolutely worth it.

I upgraded to the LG C5 55” from a Philips Ambilight TV and couldn’t be happier with the decision. The picture quality is genuinely stunning — blacks are inky deep, colours are vibrant without being over-saturated, and HDR content looks incredible. Whether it’s films, sport, or gaming, everything looks noticeably sharper and more lifelike. The brightness is excellent for an OLED and holds up well even in a bright room. Motion handling is smooth, and the upscaling of HD content is far better than I expected. Gaming performance is also top-tier with low input lag and flawless support for next-gen consoles. webOS is fast, intuitive, and far more responsive than the smart system on my previous TV. Apps load quickly and the interface is clean and easy to navigate. The design itself is sleek and premium, with incredibly thin bezels that really let the picture take centre stage. I was a bit unsure about losing Ambilight, but the sheer quality of the display more than makes up for it. This TV feels like a proper step into the high-end OLED experience. Highly recommended.

body: I chose this model because it was highly rated by Which?, to replace a TV that was 9 years old. The picture quality is the really stand-out thing compared to the TV I'm replacing: it's exceptional, vivid, and the blacks are true black. The TV definitely warrants a 5 star for picture quality.The sound is fine, it's clear and I've no complaints about the depth or bass. We don't have a soundbar, and I don't feel a need to get one.The only reason I scored the TV 4 stars rather than 5, are the menus and to some extent, the magic remote. I'm definitely tech savvy, but it's taken me a few days to find my way around fundamental functions on the TV (e.g. I found it easier to set up "favourite channels", but then it took another couple of days to figure out how to actually access "favourites"). I like the pointer on the Magic Remote, which definitely makes things easier, but the remote is let down by a very simple design flaw: both the "volume up/down" and the "channel up/down" buttons are pure black rubber. There is no visual marking on the buttons, so it's hard to see which is which. I know I'll get used to is, but in the meantime I've actually put a dab of white paint on the +/- and up/down symbols so that they are visible. The menu itself is cluttered, and there doesn't seem to be a way of hiding some the channels (e.g. I've no need for the LG channel at present, and we don't subscribe to channels like Disney, so those apps don't need to be visible on my list ... but they are, and they make it look cluttered.Overall, this is a BRILLIANT TV, and if you can put up with a cluttered menu, an overly-complex system for watching TV, and a good but imperfect remote, then I would recommend this.

body:
This review is for the 42" C55LA - Genuinely beautiful screen and picture quality. I spent ages researching this TV before buying and went to see various TV's in person in a Curry's before purchasing directly from LG online. The OLED display on the C5 looked night and day better than pretty much all of the other screens in store. It looked marginally better than the main rival's OLED display but I noticed odd flickering on the other brand's OLED on certain scenes (across various TV's) and also felt that the build and material quality of the LG C5 was significantly more premium than that of its rival at this size.The 42" is perfect for our space, and it looks awesome - super thin and really nice thin bezel. 
All in all picture quality - deep blacks - super nice with films and even standard TV - looks brilliant.The only downsides are -UK version ships with a pretty poor remote - it feels cheap and it's poorly laid out + very clunky and big. I believe the rest of the world get a nicer remote..
The OS is a bit cumbersome and bloated - there's a few tweaks to make it less so but it's still not a very nice experience. Also the remote cursor thing is genuinely annoying - you should be able to turn that off.
The other downsides are the audio quality - obviously this is a thin device but the audio is poorer than I expected it to be, and I didn't have much home in the first place + the legs that the TV stands on (42" version) are a bit flimsy but they look good.None of the downsides overshadow what is genuinely an unbelievable device with outstanding picture quality (which I find plenty bright btw). If you can get a good deal on this TV just buy it - it's a genuinely wonderful device despite its minor shortcomings.

body: After using the LG G5 TV for a month, I can honestly say it has been one of the most impressive television upgrades I have ever made. Having previously owned both an early LG Full HD flagship TV and later an LG SUHD TV, I had high expectations, but the G5 has exceeded them in every area. The first thing that stands out is the picture quality. The brightness, contrast, and colour reproduction are exceptional, delivering a viewing experience that feels incredibly lifelike. Whether watching movies, streaming series, or enjoying sports, the level of detail and sharpness is remarkable. The clarity is on another level compared to my previous TVs, making everything look cleaner, smoother, and more immersive. Even regular YouTube videos seem significantly enhanced. Another pleasant surprise has been the sound system. In the past, I often felt that TV speakers were great, with my SUHD model having Harmon Kardon speakers, but the LG G5 blows you away delivers rich, clear, and well-balanced audio. Dialogue comes through crisply, while action scenes and sporting events have a depth and presence that make them much more engaging. Although a dedicated audio system can always add more power and base, the built-in sound quality is excellent for everyday viewing and listening to music. The highlight of my first month with the TV was watching the World Cup. The experience was outstanding. The vivid colours of the pitch, the sharp detail of player movements, and the smooth handling of fast-paced action made every match feel incredibly realistic. Combined with the impressive audio, the atmosphere of the stadium came alive in my living room. The only downgrade I would say is the TV remote, whilst I have always loved the magic remotes since LG released them, I think the G5s remote is a disappointment. Overall, the LG G5 represents a huge leap forward from both my earlier LG Full HD flagship and SUHD televisions. It offers outstanding picture quality, exceptional clarity, and impressive sound performance. After one month of ownership, I am extremely satisfied and would highly recommend it to anyone looking for a premium television experience. Whilst Sony and Samsung offer great options, I believe LG are ahead of the game and would recommend LG TVs to anyone looking to purchase.

body:
I bought this OLED 65" G5 tv a week ago, upscaling from a 2024 G5 55" tv. The ⁠65-inch LG G5 OLED TV is a brilliant flagship display. It stars a Primary RGB Tandem panel with an innovative 'Brightness Booster Ultimate' and the α11 AI Processor Gen2, delivering massive brightness, peerless contrast, 165Hz gaming support, and smart webOS features.
There is incredible brightness, utilizing a 4-layer tandem design that leaps past older MLA panels, hitting extreme HDR peaks that easily rival bright-room LED options. Offering self-lit pixels providing near-infinite contrast and zero blooming around highlights. With α11 AI processing, pixel-level analysis provides pristine upscaling and sharp texture enhancement, though aggressive settings can occasionally look over-sharpened.
The tv has great design and gaming capabilities. My G5 tv includes a classy stand though it can be wall mounted for a flush, gapless wall display and has razor-thin bezel and great overall LG design uniformity. Although I don't use the tv for gaming purposes this G5 has superb gaming capabilities with 4 full-bandwidth HDMI 2.1 ports supporting 4K at 165Hz, VRR, G-Sync, and FreeSync.
The G5 has much improved audio with smart interface virtual surround, powered by a 60W 4.2-channel system utilizing AI Sound Pro to upmix audio into virtual 11.1.2 channels. I have, however, bought an LG home cinema sound system with Dolby Atmos to get the very best audio. 
The G5 runs the latest webOS 25 with deep AI personalization and is highly responsive, though the heavy menu navigation and redesigned remote (which drops the dedicated input button and the outdated number buttons) can still feel a bit cluttered. Overall, this is a superb OLED tv which delivers on all fronts.  No regrets at all in purchasing it, well worth the investment.

body: The image quality is fantastic and exactly what I expected. Bright, sharp, and genuinely impressive. Unfortunately the software experience lets it down. webOS feels limiting compared with a proper Google TV setup. I cannot install native Google TV or Android TV friendly apps, so I am forced to stick to whatever is available in the webOS app catalogue. Bluetooth audio is also fiddly. If I use an external Bluetooth speaker, after powering the TV off and back on the speaker often needs reconnecting again, which gets annoying fast. The remote is another disappointment. It has lots of shortcut buttons for apps I do not use and I find that inconvenient. Other brands offer remotes without these shortcuts, and at this price I expected more premium attention to detail. There are also missing quality of life features that are standard on Google TV, like automatically launching a chosen app after power on. Finally, I do not use cable, aerial or satellite input at all, so I do not need channel tuning or TV related menus, yet there is no option to disable that side of the interface and hide it properly. Overall, an excellent panel held back by the platform and small but constant annoyances.

Sound-wise, itÕs better than I expected for a thin TV. IÕm not saying it replaces a full sound system, but for normal watching itÕs clear, itÕs got decent punch, and dialogue doesnÕt get lost when a show decides to throw background music at you like itÕs the main character.
Also: itÕs a proper nice-looking TV. One of those that actually makes the room look better instead of just being a ********* rectangle hanging there. The design feels solid and premium.
So yeah, if you want a TV that feels like a bit of an upgrade every time you switch it on, the OLED65G56LS does that. IÕm genuinely chuffed with it.

body: I bought this TV a couple of weeks back and am absolutely *delighted* with it. The picture has to be seen to be believed and given the fact it's OLED and you get "true blacks", it's simply breathtaking!![Bearing in mind I am upgrading from a 13-year old Panasonic LED HD TV, this is a massive upgrade which blows everything out of the water. Am still very fond of my Panasonic and really liked the (Active) 3D, which sadly, is no longer a thing on TVs, but it's a sacrifice I'm willing to make and I will be keeping this TV as a secondary TV.]OK so the G5 wasn't cheap, but came with a USC9S Soundbar (which is apparently worth about £1000) and also got £200 off from a promotion, so given what I was getting, it felt like pretty good value.I'd been watching (and comparing) this other similar TVs of this spec for a few months and initially was going to settle for the 50-inch version on a stand (which does not have the tandem RGB panel BTW).However after seeing the wallmount version with its clever folding arms (into the back of the TV), we decided to go for the 55-inch (smallest wallmount version, which has the brighter panel).When it's fitted, hung and in place, it looks absolutely *fantastic* and does not dominate the room... Even compared to a 50-inch TV on a stand, or even my old 42-inch TV (also on a stand), it does not encroach, which is terrific, given the sitting room is small-medium(?) sized.However the fitting -- oh dear -- we got there in the end after 4 hours of sweating/swearing. The installation instructions, paper template & video from LG are not very good or accurate... It was only because my partner is an artist and has decades' experience of hanging exhibitions (in difficult places), that we thought we'd give it a go, but even this was not easy!!Tip for the future - for something like this, pay for the installation, because it will save you a lot of stress! We got there in the end though and managed not to drop the TV or knock it(!), but it was a tense few hours because we were terrified of damaging the screen.Setting up the TV wasn't too difficult (I should say I'm fairly techncial / IT literate), but there are a lot more options than on my previous TV (not surprising) and having a proper physical paper manual would have helped (I'm one of those sad people that does read the manual from cover to cover, just to discover all those "extras" that I might not have discovered whilst using the TV, even though I can usually work out pretty quickly how to use it).What I will say is although the default settings are OK, the colours are too vivid / unnatural (oversaturated) out of the box, especially when living with an artist who does colour for a living(!!)... This seems to be very commonplace with TVs nowadays and I've never understood why they do it -- in the shop as a demo to show what the TV is capable of, fair enough -- but at home one would want to dial the saturation down otherwise your eyes will start bleeding!!I did some research and found someone on YouTube who calibrates TVs for a living, whom I found to talk sense and be very practical. I started there by watching his videos to understand what were the main settings I needed to consider, and which of the others I could ignore.[This is not a "proper" full calibration BTW, just a few recommended settings to the ones that come out of box -- but for most people this will be more than enough.]It very quickly directed me to the different Picture Modes and advised to stick with "Film Maker Mode" (for full accuracy / fidelity to the original picture). This got the oversaturation down, but I found the picture was quite murky / too dull for my taste and having just bought an OLED TV to get a good strong/accurate picture, I didn't want it looking like my 13-year old TV (still a pretty good picture, but washed out on a lot of modern TV series and films).So then I took the settings that I'd applied to Film Maker Mode and applied them to Cinema and Standard modes... Then the picture was then good enough for me. Standard gives a colder picture; Cinema gives a warmer picture and it's the latter profile I ususally stick with as I watch TV in the evenings after work. Perhaps I'd use Standard during the day (but unlikely). These really show off the quality of the screen and the picture, without oversaturating the colours. Very very impressive.I should mention the sound too -- given how thin the TV is, it's excellent!! Having read reviews that it's tinny or "not very good", I found it to be really quite loud & powerful and certainly not tinny. Perhaps it's because it's mounted on the wall and can resonate better than the stand version, I don't know, but given the size of the sitting room and also being in a flat and I don't want to annoy the neighbours... It's absolutely fine!Another comment that has been made is that the remote is not back-lit and I would agree with that -- it's a shame as it's a very nice remote and works very well, but when I'm in the dark, I'm forever hitting the wrong button which is annoying. I guess I will learn where the buttons are by touch in the future, but right now, I either have to shine a light on the remote if in a darkened room, or keep the lights on.However I can control it from the smartphone and also I have my old Apple TV 4K (1st gen ~ 2017) which (still) works very well and I can operate the remote purely by touch. Most, if not all of what I watch is on there, so it's not a problem. Very (very!) highly recommended -- the LG G5 is quite a lot better than I expected; the picture is *fantastic*, the sound very good too, it looks really great on the wall, doesn't dominate the room and once the picture was adjusted to my taste I can honestly say I'm absolutely delighted with it! The fact you get the soundbar thrown in with it for free is excellent value too. It's very good quality and way more powerful than we'll ever need (especially in a flat -- have had to dial the bass settings right back!) and complements the TV very nicely.I've been wanting an OLED TV for a few years now and I couldn't have asked for anything better than this TV, I am extremely impressed and really delighted! Well done LG!!

Paired with an ultra-low input lag and LGÕs superb Game Optimiser dashboard, the OLED77G54LW is a weapon of choice for next-gen consoles.Design-wise, the G5 series continues its Gallery tradition: slim, flush-to-wall elegance that turns the TV into a living artwork. ItÕs stunning when off and jaw-dropping when on.The webOS experience has been cleaned up this year, offering snappier transitions and smarter recommendations without overstepping and the new _11 AI Processor? ItÕs the silent genius behind the scenes, ensuring upscaling, motion smoothing, and ambient tone mapping are all buttery-smooth and eerily lifelike.If thereÕs a flaw to be found, it's that the OLED77G54LW sets a new bar that few others can reach Ñ including LG's own previous flagships. body:
LG G5 77-inch OLED TV is a standout in LGÕs 2025 lineup, delivering exceptional performance for both cinephiles and gamers. Picture Quality
Featuring LGÕs new four-stack OLED panel, the G5 achieves peak brightness levels up to 2,300 nits in HDR mode, offering vibrant colors and deep blacks. This makes it well-suited for bright rooms and enhances HDR content dramatically.  _ _Gaming Performance

Running on webOS 25, the G5 offers a user-friendly interface with AI-driven personalization, including voice recognition and an AI chatbot for assistance.Design
The ultra-slim ÒOne WallÓ design allows for a flush wall mount, giving the TV a sleek, gallery-like appearance. Note that a stand is not included and must be purchased separately.Audio
While the built-in speakers provide decent sound with AI Sound Pro technology creating a virtual 11.1.2 channel experience, pairing the G5 with a dedicated soundbar or home theater system is recommended for optimal audio quality.Conclusion
The LG G5 77-inch OLED TV combines cutting-edge display technology, top-tier gaming features, and smart AI enhancements, making it a compelling choice for those seeking a premium home entertainment experience.

body:
After 10 years of loyal service from my trusted LG OLED55B6V, I finally decided it was time to upgrade. My old TV was brilliant, but a decade of heavy use with static TV channel logos and subtitles had eventually caused some screen burn-in.
​Moving to the OLED65G64LW has been an absolute revelation. The jump from 55 to 65 inches is impressive on its own, but the sheer leap in technology over the last ten years is mind-blowing.
​The brightness levels on this G-series panel are a massive step up from my old B6—it handles room reflections effortlessly while keeping those famous, perfect OLED blacks. Knowing how much LG has advanced their built-in panel-care features, logo luminance adjustment, and anti-burn-in tech over the years gives me massive peace of mind this time around, especially for broadcast TV and subtitles.
​The design is a work of art it mounts incredibly flush to the wall, looking completely seamless and premium. The smart webOS interface is also lightning-fast compared to older generations.
​If you are hesitating to upgrade an older OLED, don't look back. This is a masterful piece of engineering and proves why LG still leads the way.

body: Does all it says it does.

Using as a computer monitor only. Great picture quality, good brightness and lovely colours - much nicer than my old reasonably high end LCD with local dimming - no more grey patches following the cursor around the screen.

The matt coating is really good. Most of my screen is totally reflection-free, apart from one corner that reflects a patio door, where the reflection is very well muted. Extreme reflections will take on a very slightly purple tinge and the overall black level may seem slightly elevated compared to a gloss screen, but the overall Matt effect is pretty amazing , contrast is still excellent and I will never go back to gloss.

Biggest negatives are the lengthy Samsung  set up process - (I just want to plug and play - I'm not applying for a mortgage! ) and the menu system for settings: there are hundreds of them and so often, if you can even find the setting you want, it is greyed out but doesn't explain why, so you have to go looking randomly for other settings or modes to change to be able to change the setting you want.

Another problem for me using it as a monitor is that it seems to default to a home screen when it powers on - full of distracting rubbish I don't want. I want it to remember my PC input. There may be a setting for this, but I can't find it. 

Overall I'm very pleased - shame about the relatively minor negatives above.

body:
Yes great picture BUT I am still struggling to get to grips with the settings  - My previous TV was an OLED from another company from 2018 and I found that far easier to set up and then leave
I am not a techie and I really could have done with a paper manual not trying to do it electronically. For me clear concise  instructions to set up to what would serve for 90% of users as base settings would have been helpful.

I watched a documentary on IPlayer and the screen kept changing from full screen to a screen with the top and bottom missing and black ( about an inch at the top and one and half inches at the bottom). I found the same when watching live TV where some programmes were on the full screen others on the reduced screen (BBC/ITV/C5/C4)
I am not sure how to best optimise the screen settings for picture quality I know how to change them but not what would be the optimum setting for every day use
When I set up the tv and connected it to my satellite dish I tuned into Freesat but mysteriously after a day I found myself watching Samsung TV with what looks like Freeview with a whole host of extra channels. This may not be the end of the world but don't understand how or why it happened but I am assuming that as I am not receiving this through my Terrestrial aerial I will not loose the signal when raining as often happens when I used to use my Terrestrial aerial 

In fairness to Samsung I have not as yet contacted them (or the retailer) to ask for support as I have had the TV less than a week and I am still trying to work out what I really need help on - last night the screen was either full screen when I watched TV but missing the top and bottom when I was watching a recorded film . body:
**** TVS AND SUPPORT
Unfortunately, Samsung has elected to remove the QA82Q60R 82" QED from the list of TVs on which a Review can be posted. Hence my use of this space. On 29 January 2026 I sent an email to Samsung advising that our 6 yr old TV had developed a 400mm wide vertical shaded/greyed area on the right-hand side which rendered the TV unwatchable and consequently there wasn't any option but to dispose and replace. Samsung's authorised repair agent in Adelaide advised that the fault was due to either a faulty panel and/or faulty backlighting. The authorised repairer went on to advise that panels were not available, and they did not repair/replace backlighting for large screen. Consequently, the TV was not repairable.
I also advised Samsung that:
1. The Motherboard on this TV had to be replaced in the TV when it was a little short of being three years old
2. Our current TV was purchased to replace our previous 65" Samsung which had to be disposed of after 5yrs due to unrepairable lines appearing on the screen. Samsung was not prepared to assist us at the time.

Despite the fact that this is the second Samsung TV which has died and deemed to be unrepairable within a ten to eleven year period, Samsung Customer Care refused to assist us in any way and advised that 5 to six years was considered to be a reasonable lifetime for their TV's.

I then lodged a complaint via email to the CEO's office and received the same response. I followed up this response on 13/2/26 and proposed a solution under which Samsung sold us a replacement TV at a discounted price. When I had not received the courtesy of a reply by 17/2/26 I sent a follow email. As at the date of this review viz 4/3/26 I have still not received a reply to either of these emails.

While I acknowledge that technically both TV's were out of warranty, it is fair and reasonable to expect that high end expensive TV's would have a life in excess of 10 years and in addition would be repairable for periods up to and in excess of this. Unfortunately, Samsung has failed to demonstrate any responsibility for their defective products or corporate conscious. In addition, they appear to endorse a "disposable" environmentally unfriendly culture.

body: One word - Excellent .I am very pleased and happy with everything about it.

I bought this TV to replace an old 19" Panasonic TV that has been in our kitchen for about 20 years.  Because the bezel surround is so much smaller than the old TV, although the screen is 24", it's hardly any larger than the old TV in overall dimensions.  Setup was straightforward (I already have an Amazon account).  Picture is fine, sound is OK - good enough for a small room, but I might need a soundbar to improve the sound in due course.  Wide choice of channels and apps.  All the usual.  For what we want it for - watching TV at the kitchen table - its fine.  Some gripes or niggles.  The home screen is confusing and can't be changed.  The use manual that comes with the set is minimal - you have to download the full manual from Panasonic (I've printed it off).  Every time you turn it on it asks who is using the TV - you don't appear to be be to set it to remember this.  I have saved a number of channels as favourites but there doesn't seem to be a way of only displaying favourite channels.  Indeed, I struggle to work out what purpose saving channels as favourites has.  The function for changing the order in which channels appear does not appear to work. Navigation between channels is clunky. We live on the border of two regions - Midlands and West.  BBC Midlands displays in the main channel list, but BBC West only displays in BBC iPlayer.  Switching between the two involves a complicated navigation, and I can't find a way of having them next to each other in the channel guide.  Ditto ITV Midlands and West.  So although this a very good TV, I have deducted one star for poor instructions, a complicated home screen and clunky navigation.

body: I recently owned a TCL C6K and a TCL C7K and I can confidently say this Panasonic W95B mini LED TV delivers exceptional picture quality and colour. While the TCLs boast Quantum Dots, the Panasonic doesn’t, but you wouldn’t notice. Simply set the colour to auto and you’ll get cinema-standard colours. They’re bright, punchy yet not overly saturated. Grass appears realistic, skies look natural and water looks clear with a subtle blue tint, as if you’re looking at it in person rather than on a TV. It performs in ways the TCLs simply couldn’t. Don’t get me wrong, I loved the TCLs, but I had a screen issue so I had to return them. I’m too impatient to wait for them to come back in stock, so I took the gamble on the Panasonic. Movies on the Panasonic are more like being in a cinema compared to the TCLs, which simply tried to impress with contrast. Don’t get me wrong, sometimes the incredible contrast was a strong point, but at times it was just a bit much on the eyes. Blacks were probably better on the C7K, but I felt it did come with slight black crush and blooming control. I’d have to hand it to the TCLs for having more zones, which usually results in better blooming control unless you have an OLED (which I also own). By no means is the Panasonic bad; it really isn’t, and I have it in an 85-inch model and barely notice it. However, depending on the content and the scene, it’s just a tad more noticeable. I thought I’d hate the fact that it runs on the Fire OS, but it’s actually very snappy and I haven’t had an issue with it. I also own a Fire Stick 4K Max and it’s significantly slower than the Panasonic’s built-in Fire OS, so they did a good job with it. Everyone raved about the TCLs in 2025 for good reason; they pack a lot of spec into an affordable TV. However, after having multiple units between the C6K and the C7K (four) and experiencing issues with all of them, I switched to a brand that was an old-school flagship manufacturer and it has delivered! I’m certain this is the hidden gem that 2025 had to offer. However, as I mentioned, everything revolved around TCL and they stole the spotlight, leaving this TV with minimal reviews. If you get the chance to purchase it you won’t be disappointed. Unlike my four TCLs, I only have one Panasonic and I can’t fault it. Just to add I compared this more against the C7K as it hands down beats the C6 in every area.

The FIRE tv app is ok.  Slow to load, but once it's going, it's good.  So we pop the telly on via remote command, and go make a cuppa.

body:
Amazing TV, but. - I had the Z95A and it had 2 major problems. First was, that after I connected my external sound system, the internal speakers stopped working completely , even after it was turned off/disconnected again. The only option to get them to work again was a factory reset. This problem couldn't be resolved by the support. The second, more serious problem was, that there's been posterisation and banding especially within some Dolby vision content. body: I recently owned a TCL C6K and a TCL C7K and I can confidently say this Panasonic W95B mini LED TV delivers exceptional picture quality and colour. While the TCLs boast Quantum Dots, the Panasonic doesn’t, but you wouldn’t notice. Simply set the colour to auto and you’ll get cinema-standard colours. They’re bright, punchy yet not overly saturated. Grass appears realistic, skies look natural and water looks clear with a subtle blue tint, as if you’re looking at it in person rather than on a TV. It performs in ways the TCLs simply couldn’t. Don’t get me wrong, I loved the TCLs, but I had a screen issue so I had to return them. I’m too impatient to wait for them to come back in stock, so I took the gamble on the Panasonic. Movies on the Panasonic are more like being in a cinema compared to the TCLs, which simply tried to impress with contrast. Don’t get me wrong, sometimes the incredible contrast was a strong point, but at times it was just a bit much on the eyes. Blacks were probably better on the C7K, but I felt it did come with slight black crush and blooming control. I’d have to hand it to the TCLs for having more zones, which usually results in better blooming control unless you have an OLED (which I also own). By no means is the Panasonic bad; it really isn’t, and I have it in an 85-inch model and barely notice it. However, depending on the content and the scene, it’s just a tad more noticeable. I thought I’d hate the fact that it runs on the Fire OS, but it’s actually very snappy and I haven’t had an issue with it. I also own a Fire Stick 4K Max and it’s significantly slower than the Panasonic’s built-in Fire OS, so they did a good job with it. Everyone raved about the TCLs in 2025 for good reason; they pack a lot of spec into an affordable TV. However, after having multiple units between the C6K and the C7K (four) and experiencing issues with all of them, I switched to a brand that was an old-school flagship manufacturer and it has delivered! body:
Amazing TV, but. - I had the Z95A and it had 2 major problems. First was, that after I connected my external sound system, the internal speakers stopped working completely , even after it was turned off/disconnected again. The only option to get them to work again was a factory reset. This problem couldn't be resolved by the support. The second, more serious problem was, that there's been posterisation and banding especially within some Dolby vision content. This problem wasn't addressed in  any of the available tests and other sources regarding the Z95A. But it was mentioned in 2 tests of the Z95B. The fact that the Z95B still has this problem apparently means, that Panasonic wasn't able to fix it within 1,5 years and therefore it will most probably persist. There's been at least one user who reported the same sound problem and one who reported the  same picture problems with the Z95B. When I suggested to exchange the Z95A with the Z95B, Panasonic refunded me instead. Without these flaws the Z95 would be the best TV available on the market, especially because the LG G5 has a lot more problems, which LG hasn't been able to fix so far. There's no doubt, that the Z95B is an amazing TV and still the best option to go for at the moment. 
It's a shame that Panasonic will retreat from the European market by March 26, due to poor sales figures! Thank you Panasonic for decades of top notch home entertainment! 
I added some photos showing the picture problems.

body: I recently owned a TCL C6K and a TCL C7K and I can confidently say this Panasonic W95B mini LED TV delivers exceptional picture quality and colour. While the TCLs boast Quantum Dots, the Panasonic doesn’t, but you wouldn’t notice. Simply set the colour to auto and you’ll get cinema-standard colours. They’re bright, punchy yet not overly saturated. Grass appears realistic, skies look natural and water looks clear with a subtle blue tint, as if you’re looking at it in person rather than on a TV. It performs in ways the TCLs simply couldn’t. Don’t get me wrong, I loved the TCLs, but I had a screen issue so I had to return them. I’m too impatient to wait for them to come back in stock, so I took the gamble on the Panasonic. Movies on the Panasonic are more like being in a cinema compared to the TCLs, which simply tried to impress with contrast. Don’t get me wrong, sometimes the incredible contrast was a strong point, but at times it was just a bit much on the eyes. Blacks were probably better on the C7K, but I felt it did come with slight black crush and blooming control. I’d have to hand it to the TCLs for having more zones, which usually results in better blooming control unless you have an OLED (which I also own). By no means is the Panasonic bad; it really isn’t, and I have it in an 85-inch model and barely notice it. However, depending on the content and the scene, it’s just a tad more noticeable. I thought I’d hate the fact that it runs on the Fire OS, but it’s actually very snappy and I haven’t had an issue with it. I also own a Fire Stick 4K Max and it’s significantly slower than the Panasonic’s built-in Fire OS, so they did a good job with it. Everyone raved about the TCLs in 2025 for good reason; they pack a lot of spec into an affordable TV. However, after having multiple units between the C6K and the C7K (four) and experiencing issues with all of them, I switched to a brand that was an old-school flagship manufacturer and it has delivered! I’m certain this is the hidden gem that 2025 had to offer. However, as I mentioned, everything revolved around TCL and they stole the spotlight, leaving this TV with minimal reviews. If you get the chance to purchase it you won’t be disappointed. Unlike my four TCLs, I only have one Panasonic and I can’t fault it. Just to add I compared this more against the C7K as it hands down beats the C6 in every area.

First was, that after I connected my external sound system, the internal speakers stopped working completely , even after it was turned off/disconnected again. The only option to get them to work again was a factory reset. This problem couldn't be resolved by the support. The second, more serious problem was, that there's been posterisation and banding especially within some Dolby vision content. This problem wasn't addressed in  any of the available tests and other sources regarding the Z95A. But it was mentioned in 2 tests of the Z95B. The fact that the Z95B still has this problem apparently means, that Panasonic wasn't able to fix it within 1,5 years and therefore it will most probably persist. There's been at least one user who reported the same sound problem and one who reported the  same picture problems with the Z95B. When I suggested to exchange the Z95A with the Z95B, Panasonic refunded me instead. Without these flaws the Z95 would be the best TV available on the market, especially because the LG G5 has a lot more problems, which LG hasn't been able to fix so far. There's no doubt, that the Z95B is an amazing TV and still the best option to go for at the moment. 
It's a shame that Panasonic will retreat from the European market by March 26, due to poor sales figures! Thank you Panasonic for decades of top notch home entertainment! 
I added some photos showing the picture problems.

body: I recently owned a TCL C6K and a TCL C7K and I can confidently say this Panasonic W95B mini LED TV delivers exceptional picture quality and colour. While the TCLs boast Quantum Dots, the Panasonic doesn’t, but you wouldn’t notice. Simply set the colour to auto and you’ll get cinema-standard colours. They’re bright, punchy yet not overly saturated. Grass appears realistic, skies look natural and water looks clear with a subtle blue tint, as if you’re looking at it in person rather than on a TV. It performs in ways the TCLs simply couldn’t. Don’t get me wrong, I loved the TCLs, but I had a screen issue so I had to return them. I’m too impatient to wait for them to come back in stock, so I took the gamble on the Panasonic. Movies on the Panasonic are more like being in a cinema compared to the TCLs, which simply tried to impress with contrast. Don’t get me wrong, sometimes the incredible contrast was a strong point, but at times it was just a bit much on the eyes. Blacks were probably better on the C7K, but I felt it did come with slight black crush and blooming control. I’d have to hand it to the TCLs for having more zones, which usually results in better blooming control unless you have an OLED (which I also own). By no means is the Panasonic bad; it really isn’t, and I have it in an 85-inch model and barely notice it. However, depending on the content and the scene, it’s just a tad more noticeable. I thought I’d hate the fact that it runs on the Fire OS, but it’s actually very snappy and I haven’t had an issue with it. I also own a Fire Stick 4K Max and it’s significantly slower than the Panasonic’s built-in Fire OS, so they did a good job with it. Everyone raved about the TCLs in 2025 for good reason; they pack a lot of spec into an affordable TV. However, after having multiple units between the C6K and the C7K (four) and experiencing issues with all of them, I switched to a brand that was an old-school flagship manufacturer and it has delivered! I’m certain this is the hidden gem that 2025 had to offer. However, as I mentioned, everything revolved around TCL and they stole the spotlight, leaving this TV with minimal reviews. If you get the chance to purchase it you won’t be disappointed. Unlike my four TCLs, I only have one Panasonic and I can’t fault it. Just to add I compared this more against the C7K as it hands down beats the C6 in every area.

body: I recently owned a TCL C6K and a TCL C7K and I can confidently say this Panasonic W95B mini LED TV delivers exceptional picture quality and colour. While the TCLs boast Quantum Dots, the Panasonic doesn’t, but you wouldn’t notice. Simply set the colour to auto and you’ll get cinema-standard colours. They’re bright, punchy yet not overly saturated. Grass appears realistic, skies look natural and water looks clear with a subtle blue tint, as if you’re looking at it in person rather than on a TV. It performs in ways the TCLs simply couldn’t. Don’t get me wrong, I loved the TCLs, but I had a screen issue so I had to return them. I’m too impatient to wait for them to come back in stock, so I took the gamble on the Panasonic. Movies on the Panasonic are more like being in a cinema compared to the TCLs, which simply tried to impress with contrast. Don’t get me wrong, sometimes the incredible contrast was a strong point, but at times it was just a bit much on the eyes. Blacks were probably better on the C7K, but I felt it did come with slight black crush and blooming control. I’d have to hand it to the TCLs for having more zones, which usually results in better blooming control unless you have an OLED (which I also own). By no means is the Panasonic bad; it really isn’t, and I have it in an 85-inch model and barely notice it. However, depending on the content and the scene, it’s just a tad more noticeable. I thought I’d hate the fact that it runs on the Fire OS, but it’s actually very snappy and I haven’t had an issue with it. I also own a Fire Stick 4K Max and it’s significantly slower than the Panasonic’s built-in Fire OS, so they did a good job with it. Everyone raved about the TCLs in 2025 for good reason; they pack a lot of spec into an affordable TV. However, after having multiple units between the C6K and the C7K (four) and experiencing issues with all of them, I switched to a brand that was an old-school flagship manufacturer and it has delivered! I’m certain this is the hidden gem that 2025 had to offer. However, as I mentioned, everything revolved around TCL and they stole the spotlight, leaving this TV with minimal reviews. If you get the chance to purchase it you won’t be disappointed. Unlike my four TCLs, I only have one Panasonic and I can’t fault it. Just to add I compared this more against the C7K as it hands down beats the C6 in every area.

body: Good for the money, simple as that

We needed a TV for the kitchen and also our bedroom and purchased 2 Samsung models. This larger one is in our bedroom and it’s a great TV for the price. Unboxing was a methodical experience and it was easy to attach the stand and other parts. The TV is very stable on 2 small feet and sits low on a surface; the minimal bezel is barely noticeable. 

Setup was fairly straight forward; I tend to dislike the “Home” screen landing pages on TV’s but it was easy to change so it defaulted to the SkyTV channels instead. The remote is fiddly; buttons are small and therefore any writing on them is also small. However we set our Sky remote to manage volume etc., so will have minimal use of the Samsung remote.  Setting the usual things such as brightness, contrast etc was easily done via the Samsung interface. You can add Apps for the most common services such as Netflix, Amazon Prime, Disney etc but you need to give password details to allow that. 

I love that pressing the “on” button on our Sky remote switches both the Sky box and the TV on. The TV is slow to respond to the Sky interface with a noticeable delay when changing channels. Worst case scenario results in a black screen for 10 seconds or so, which doesn’t sound like much but can quickly become frustrating. We have no such problems with the 24” version in our kitchen. 

The picture is very clear with the matte finish on the screen reducing glare from windows. In terms of picture quality, there is minimal pixelation (blocky squares) when showing very black/dark environments onscreen. 

All in all, it’s a great TV and perfect for midsized rooms, gaming and similar.

It’s ok. The picture is good and downloading/playing apps was fine. It’s just SLOW! The processor can’t seem to cope with even simple commands quickly.  Very frustrating. And watching live tv is a nightmare, it’s like it was added as an afterthought. I couldn’t get terrestrial HD either. A little disappointing.

body: This is my first OLED TV, replacing a 13 year old Panasonic Viera plasma, and I have been stunned at the improvement in picture quality from what was a very good TV in its day. I use an Apple TV 4K as my source, run through an Anthem AVM90 processor to the A95L, and it integrates perfectly. All the positives of OLED and the Bravia XR Processor are very evident, from the picture clarity, colour/tone "realism", to the deep blacks, to the quality of upscaling, etc. Compared to other high-end OLEDs (S95F, G5) the picture and colour/tone really is more realistic / less saturated.  I wanted a 77" screen, and so spent a long time debating whether to buy the A95L (arguably an older model) or a more recent TV from other brands.  The feature that the reviews keep coming back to is that newer TVs have higher picture brightness, "peak nits", etc, but all I can say is that the A95L is as bright as I would want.  Watching documentaries such as Our Planet on Netflix in Dolby Vision, I have found myself squinting when bright sunlight is coming into the camera !  A friend has the Bravia 8ii OLED and while I obviously haven't done a side-by-side comparison, I can't see any improvement on the A95L in normal viewing. The A95L might be an "older model" these days, but if you are looking for a 77" OLED I would strongly recommend that you buy it: all the reasons why everyone raved about it in 2023/24 are still there, and the fact it doesn't have the peak brightness of modern OLEDs or RGB LED is in my view irrelevant.

body: My old TV (another company) was starting to have issues and needed replacing.  I've never owned a Sony flat TV before but did a lot of research. In most professional reviews the A95L comes out on top. My biggest issue was to work out which sony to go for in the 55 size as there are several options. After a lot of thinking I went for this one and after a few weeks I don't regret the decision! Yes this TV carries a premium price over over brands and Sony's other options, however it's a true powerhouse and several steps up from the old OLED we had. Setting up took a little time (I put it on the higher stand setting as we are using a soundbar). Picture quality; off the charts. I did change some settings, mainly the picture to professional mode and increase the motion settings and adjust the HDR. We've tested it on several feeds, including sky, ps5 and steaming. This TV really sings when you feed it proper HD blu rays. Not only the natural quality of the colours and the depth of the blacks, but also the highlights. As well as looking much sharper it's the colours where we feel we see a huge step up. You notice far more details on films and they look almost 3D (must be the depth of colours and HDR). The sound is also incredible. They have developed almost physics defying technology on this TV where good sound comes through the screen. Even without a sound system it sounds great. We actually connect it to our Sony soundbar and it works a treat in the broader setup as a central panel. Ease of use; I was a little worried beforehand that this TV was google powered however since turning it on we've had no issues. It's responsive and aggregates all your apps and feeds into one place and the 'google' bit doesn't interfere with our daily use. This connectivity is also a another step up for us. Build quality; has a real premium feel to it. Minimal design but the physical properties of the TV do shine. There are lots of options and things to do to improve it (such as panels to cover wires once you have plugged them in). Comes with two remotes and an optional camera module you can plug in (which as great as we don't want to use it). The main remote is cool and has a premium feel including shortcuts to key streaming apps. Games; the ps5 performance is incredible. Includes 120hz support and VRR meaning you can explore new options in games (eg. 120 and 40fps). The TV importantly can also ring fence settings to each input which is a game changer for me (eg. You can manually optimise settings for sky, ps5 and blu ray etc.). And when using ps5 there's a special game feature quick access setting feature. Connectivity; connects to WiFi, Bluetooth and various apps etc. inc Google as well as physically uses an e-arc port which means we can control most things through the single remote. One important comment, all of the TV inputs are on the left side of the tv when you look at it (versus right on my other panels) meaning we had to buy some new longer cables. Also includes 2 hdmi 2.1 ports so something to consider in your set up. Make sure you get proper hdmi 2.1 cables if you want to use the ps5 properly and invest in HD blu rays to really see what 4k looks like. It's re ignited my interest in watching films again! The TV also has a deal where you can access Sony's own streaming app, which unsurprisingly is vastly higher quality than the mainstream ones. However this is limited to (Sony?) films only. With the additional Sony sound system set up we bought (under a bundle deal) watching properly optimised 4k movies is incredible, we likely won't be going to the cinema again! In summary, it's a powerhouse of a TV and we look forward to watching more content on it.

body: My old TV (another company) was starting to have issues and needed replacing.  I've never owned a Sony flat TV before but did a lot of research. In most professional reviews the A95L comes out on top. My biggest issue was to work out which sony to go for in the 55 size as there are several options. After a lot of thinking I went for this one and after a few weeks I don't regret the decision! Yes this TV carries a premium price over over brands and Sony's other options however it's a true powerhouse and several steps up from the old OLED we had. Setting up took a little time (I put it on the higher stand setting as we are using a soundbar). Picture quality; off the charts. I did change some settings mainly the picture to professional mode and increase the motion settings and adjust the HDR. We've tested it on several feeds including sky ps5 and steaming. This TV really sings when you feed it proper HD blu rays. Not only the natural quality of the colours and the depth of the blacks but also the highlights. As well as looking much sharper it's the colours where we feel we see a huge step up. You notice far more details on films and they look almost 3D (must be the depth of colours and HDR). The sound is also incredible. They have developed almost physics defying technology on this TV where good sound comes through the screen. Even without a sound system it sounds great. We actually connect it to our Sony soundbar and it works a treat in the broader setup as a central panel. Ease of use; I was a little worried beforehand that this TV was google powered however since turning it on we've had no issues. It's responsive and aggregates all your apps and feeds into one place and the 'google' bit doesn't interfere with our daily use. This connectivity is also a another step up for us. Build quality; has a real premium feel to it. Minimal design but the physical properties of the TV do shine. There are lots of options and things to do to improve it (such as panels to cover wires once you have plugged them in). Comes with two remotes and an optional camera module you can plug in (which as great as we don't want to use it). The main remote is cool and has a premium feel including shortcuts to key streaming apps. Games; the ps5 performance is incredible. Includes 120hz support and VRR meaning you can explore new options in games (eg. 120 and 40fps). The TV importantly can also ring fence settings to each input which is a game changer for me (eg. You can manually optimise settings for sky ps5 and blu ray etc.). And when using ps5 there's a special game feature quick access setting feature. Connectivity; connects to WiFi Bluetooth and various apps etc. inc Google as well as physically uses an e-arc port which means we can control most things through the single remote. One important comment all of the TV inputs are on the left side of the tv when you look at it (versus right on my other panels) meaning we had to buy some new longer cables. Also includes 2 hdmi 2.1 ports so something to consider in your set up. Make sure you get proper hdmi 2.1 cables if you want to use the ps5 properly and invest in HD blu rays to really see what 4k looks like. It's re ignited my interest in watching films again! The TV also has a deal where you can access Sony's own streaming app which unsurprisingly is vastly higher quality than the mainstream ones. However this is limited to (Sony?) films only. With the additional Sony sound system set up we bought (under a bundle deal) watching properly optimised 4k movies is incredible we likely won't be going to the cinema again! In summary it's a powerhouse of a TV and we look forward to watching more content on it.
